lesson.title: TLS: The Hybrid Design That Makes the Web Trustworthy
lesson.summary: TLS is the protocol that secures data in transit on top of TCP, combining nearly everything covered so far in this unit by using slower asymmetric cryptography and X.509 certificates just once to authenticate the server and agree on a key, then switching to fast symmetric encryption for the actual data.
lesson.body:
TLS, Transport Layer Security, descends from an earlier protocol called SSL, and has since been standardized and evolved through a series of IETF RFCs. The current version, TLS 1.3, is specified in RFC 8446 and is the version this unit's handshake chapter walks through in detail; TLS 1.2 is still commonly encountered, while older SSL and early TLS versions are now considered insecure and have been deprecated across modern browsers and servers. TLS conventionally runs as a layer sitting above TCP, providing security to whatever application protocol rides on top of it, though it is worth a brief mention that newer transport designs like QUIC apply TLS 1.3's cryptography over UDP instead, a detail that goes beyond what this unit covers.

The single idea worth holding onto through the rest of this unit is that TLS is not built around one kind of cryptography, it is a deliberate hybrid of everything covered in the past several chapters. Symmetric encryption is fast but cannot solve how two parties who have never met agree on a key. Public key cryptography solves exactly that key agreement problem but is too computationally expensive to use for encrypting large volumes of data. TLS resolves this by using public key operations, with the server's identity backed by an X.509 certificate issued and signed through the CA chain of trust covered in the previous two chapters, only briefly, during a handshake at the very start of the connection, purely to authenticate the server and derive a fresh symmetric session key. Every byte of actual application data that follows, the contents of a webpage, an API response, a file download, is then protected using a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 with that freshly derived key. Almost nothing about TLS makes sense without recognizing that split.

Within the handshake, client and server also negotiate a cipher suite, a bundled agreement covering which key exchange algorithm, which symmetric cipher, and which mechanism for integrity checking will be used for this particular connection. The client offers a list of cipher suites it supports, typically in order of preference, and the server selects one that both sides support, which packages together several of the individual building blocks from earlier chapters into a single negotiated choice rather than agreeing on each piece separately.

TLS 1.3 specifically removed a number of older, weaker options that had accumulated over the protocol's history. Among the more significant changes, it dropped support for static RSA key exchange, an older approach that did not provide forward secrecy, in favor of requiring ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange for every connection. Forward secrecy is a property worth naming explicitly: because each connection generates a brand new, temporary key exchange value that is discarded afterward, even if a server's long term private key were somehow stolen later, an attacker who had recorded past encrypted sessions still could not go back and decrypt them, since those sessions never depended on the long term key directly for their symmetric session keys. Exactly how the handshake plays out message by message, and how that ephemeral key exchange actually happens, is the subject of the final chapter in this unit; how all of this looks from the outside, wrapping ordinary web traffic, is the subject of the next one.
